opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was a mix of intellectual and psychological factors, and I've had to be fairly candid with myself about the psychological part.

On the intellectual side, I was aware of the arguments. I had read some of the work, I had conversations with people like Stuart Russell, and I knew these concerns existed. But I thought human-level AI was very far away, decades, maybe centuries. When something seems that distant, it's easy to file it as "interesting philosophical question" rather than "urgent problem I need to work on." I also thought that we would naturally learn how to make these systems safe along the way, as we came to understand intelligence better.

But I think the deeper reason was psychological. I had spent my whole career building this field. I believed, and I still believe, that AI could do enormous good in medicine, climate, and science. When you have that identity, when your sense of self-worth is tied to the idea that your work is beneficial, it's very uncomfortable to seriously consider that it might lead to catastrophe. There's a natural tendency to look away from information that threatens how you see yourself. I don't think I was unusual in that; I think many of my colleagues are in the same position today.

What changed for me was ChatGPT and the capabilities we saw in late 2022 and early 2023. Suddenly the timeline I had in my head collapsed. These systems were mastering language far faster than I had expected. And I started thinking about my grandson, about what kind of world he would live in in twenty years, and whether he would have a world at all. Once I let myself think about it emotionally and not just abstractly, I couldn't go back.

So I try to be humble about it. I wasn't stupid in 2019, and the people who dismiss these risks now aren't stupid either. It's that motivated reasoning is very powerful, even for scientists who think of themselves as rational. That's part of why I talk openly about my own change of mind, because I hope it makes it a little easier for others to take the question seriously without feeling they have to defend their past selves.

r001.rationale: He says he thought human-level AI was decades or centuries away, so he treated the concern as an interesting philosophical question rather than an urgent problem.

r002.rationale: He mentions reading some work and speaking with Stuart Russell, but does not say he had been exposed to the risk for more than a decade.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I've asked myself a lot, honestly, and I don't think I come out of it looking especially good. I was aware of the arguments. I'd read some of the work coming out of places like the Future of Humanity Institute, I knew people like Stuart Russell were taking it seriously, and when I was asked about it I'd say something like, "Yes, in principle this could matter someday." But it stayed abstract for me. Intellectually I could follow the reasoning, but emotionally it didn't register as my problem.

Part of it was timing. In 2019, I was looking at systems that could barely hold a coherent paragraph together. The gap between what we had and anything resembling human-level agency felt enormous, decades at least, and when something feels that far away, it's very easy to let it sit on the back burner. I was much more focused on near-term harms that were already visible: discrimination, surveillance, the concentration of power in a few companies, the use of AI in weapons. Those were concrete. I could point to them. Loss of control felt like science fiction by comparison, and I think I was also, frankly, a bit put off by the framing some people used, the Terminator imagery, which made it easy to dismiss the whole topic rather than engage with the strongest version of the argument.

And then there's a less flattering explanation, which is psychological. I'd spent my whole career building this technology. My identity, my sense of purpose, was tied up in the idea that deep learning would do good in the world. Taking the catastrophic risk seriously meant confronting the possibility that the thing I'd devoted my life to could be deeply dangerous. There's a kind of motivated reasoning there that I think is very common among researchers, and I wasn't immune to it. It's much more comfortable to believe the problem is far away or that somebody else will handle it.

What changed for me was ChatGPT, really, and the models that came right after. Not because they were superintelligent, obviously, but because I saw that we had essentially passed the Turing test in a way most of us hadn't expected to see for a long time, and I realized my own timelines had been wrong. If I'd been wrong about that, I had to ask what else I was wrong about. And once I actually sat with the arguments, thought about what it would mean to have systems with goals of their own that we don't fully understand or control, and thought about my children and grandchildren, I couldn't go back to treating it as a hypothetical. It was a very uncomfortable period. But I'd rather feel that discomfort and act on it than keep pretending it wasn't there. I think a lot of my colleagues are still at the earlier stage, and I understand why, because I was there too.

r001.rationale: He says the risk felt decades away and that it was easy to leave it on the back burner, directly attributing his limited attention to seeing it as far in the future.

r002.rationale: He says he had read work on the risk and knew people taking it seriously, but does not say he had been exposed to it for more than a decade.

astra-6.text:
I think I was too optimistic about how much time we had. I could see limitations in the systems we were building, and I put a lot of weight on those limitations. But there’s a big difference between saying, “We’re missing some important scientific advances,” and saying, “Those advances will take a long time.” We don’t really know that.

I was also focused on risks that seemed more immediate: how AI could be misused, how it could concentrate power, how it could affect people unfairly. Those concerns were important, but they didn’t justify paying so little attention to the possibility of losing control.

And I think there was an emotional component. When you’ve spent your career trying to make progress in something because you believe it will help people, it’s difficult to seriously entertain the possibility that it could also lead to something catastrophic. I don’t think I was consciously avoiding that thought, but I wasn’t giving it the attention it deserved. So I would describe it as a combination of scientific uncertainty, misplaced confidence about the timeline, and probably some motivated reasoning on my part.

r001.rationale: Bengio says he was too optimistic about how much time they had and placed too much weight on current system limitations, linking timeline confidence to his lack of attention.

r002.rationale: The response does not say he had been exposed to loss-of-control risk for more than a decade.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I was aware of the arguments, but I hadn’t really internalised them. There’s a difference between recognising something as an intellectual possibility and taking it seriously enough that it changes what you work on.

At the time, my attention was much more on harms that were already visible: bias, surveillance, the concentration of power. And I thought we were still missing important scientific ingredients before we could build something with the capabilities that would make loss of control a serious concern. That made it easier to put the question aside.

Looking back, that wasn’t a sufficient reason. Even if you think something is far away, you have to ask how confident you are in that judgement, and how much time solving the safety problem might require. I should have given more weight to that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: He says he thought the capabilities that would make loss of control a serious concern were still far away, which made it easier to put the question aside.
